mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Louis XVI—coronation and sacred kingship
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The 1775 coronation joined sacral legitimacy and inherited ritual obligations to a monarchy whose forms had accumulated unevenly over time.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The author treats the ceremony as emotionally powerful but also as a mixture of meaningful authority, empty form, and court distraction.
successor_labels: Louis XVI—coronation and sacred kingship

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: France—territorial composition and enclaves
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The kingdom was an accretion of provinces acquired through conquest and dynastic succession, with foreign and papal enclaves still embedded within it.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Territorial irregularities were historically legitimate to contemporaries rather than self-evident anomalies.
successor_labels: France—territorial composition and enclaves

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: France—overlapping administrative, judicial, and ecclesiastical divisions
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Provinces, generalities, intendancies, parlementary ressorts, archiepiscopal provinces, and dioceses overlapped and generated recurrent jurisdictional conflict.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The pattern was uneven and illogical in appearance, yet historically rooted and central to how the kingdom functioned.
successor_labels: France—overlapping administrative, judicial, and ecclesiastical divisions

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: France—legal, fiscal, and commercial fragmentation
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Customary and Roman law, weights and measures, direct taxes, the gabelle, tolls, and internal customs varied sharply by locality.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The fragmentation impeded exchange and invited fraud, litigation, and unequal burdens, although it often reflected geography, culture, and historical bargains.
successor_labels: France—legal, fiscal, and commercial fragmentation

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Paris basin—metropolitan integration
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Navigable rivers, superior roads, fertile commercial agriculture, literacy, French language, and access to Paris made the basin the kingdom's most integrated and governable core.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The region's advantages were exceptional and could not be generalized beyond roughly 150 miles from the capital.
successor_labels: Paris basin—metropolitan integration

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: France—regional diversity and uneven integration
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Contrasting landscapes, languages, communications, economies, religious communities, and provincial institutions made France a set of distinct regional worlds.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Regional diversity is structural, not decorative background; central authority and market integration weakened with distance and terrain.
successor_labels: France—regional diversity and uneven integration

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Brittany and the Vendée—society, autonomy, and economy
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The western bocage contained distinctive Breton language and provincial autonomy, major Atlantic ports, and the relatively isolated subsistence economy of the Vendée.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Brittany combined poverty in appearance with population, low taxation, self-government, roads, and global commerce; the Vendée was more inward-looking.
successor_labels: Brittany and the Vendée—society, autonomy, and economy

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: South-western France and Bordeaux—agriculture and commerce
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The Garonne basin supported diverse agriculture, maize, petty cultivation, and sharecropping, while Bordeaux became an exceptional Atlantic commercial metropolis.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Good communications and fertile land did not make the region's agriculture as commercialized as the north; Bordeaux's boom stood apart.
successor_labels: South-western France and Bordeaux—agriculture and commerce

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Languedoc and the Midi—environment, autonomy, and Protestantism
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Mediterranean climate, the Massif Central, Occitan speech, provincial institutions, and a large persecuted Protestant population distinguished southern France.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Terrain and autonomous traditions limited central power, while the memory of Camisard rebellion and the Calas affair sustained sectarian tension.
successor_labels: Languedoc and the Midi—environment, autonomy, and Protestantism

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Eastern and Rhône-Saône France—regional economies and frontiers
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The Rhône corridor linked Provence and the north; Dauphiné, Lyons, Burgundy, Lorraine, Franche-Comté, and Alsace exhibited distinct economies, institutions, religions, and orientations.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Economic dynamism clustered around ports, routes, silk, wine, and emerging industry, while mountains and recent annexations preserved strong local separateness.
successor_labels: Eastern and Rhône-Saône France—regional economies and frontiers

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: French agriculture—low productivity and fragmented peasant property
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Conservative technology, partible inheritance, morcellation, small ownership, and piecemeal leasing constrained productivity and marketable surplus.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The author broadly accepts contemporary diagnoses of backwardness but explains the rational pressures behind small-scale cultivation and sharecropping.
successor_labels: French agriculture—low productivity and fragmented peasant property

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Agriculture—crop systems, fallow, and regional innovation
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Dependence on grain, weak livestock and manure supplies, and extensive fallow limited yields, while maize, potatoes, and fodder rotations succeeded in particular regions.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Innovation was possible where ecological shock or strong urban markets created incentives, but remained geographically restricted.
successor_labels: Agriculture—crop systems, fallow, and regional innovation

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Commercial farming—Paris basin and gros fermiers
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Urban demand around Paris and Flanders supported large leases, capital-intensive cultivation, and prosperous tenant farmers.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Commercial farmers improved market supply but disrupted village access to land, commons, gleaning, and customary rights.
successor_labels: Commercial farming—Paris basin and gros fermiers

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Agriculture—taxes, tithes, corvée, and feudal burdens
mapping_rows.old_meaning: State taxation, tithe, road labor, and seigneurial rights absorbed substantial shares of agricultural output and limited investment.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Burdens varied enormously by place; 'feudalism' is used as a contemporary umbrella for a complex mix of dues and rights rather than a uniform system.
successor_labels: Agriculture—taxes, tithes, corvée, and feudal burdens

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Seigneurial rights and rural tenure
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Cens, dues in cash or kind, hunting rights, banalités, and manorial courts survived after lordship and ownership had largely separated.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Tenures blended feudal and contractual elements so thoroughly that later revolutionary attempts to classify them would be consequential and contentious.
successor_labels: Seigneurial rights and rural tenure

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Agriculture under Louis XVI—harvest instability and rural crisis
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Mid-century prosperity gave way after the late 1760s to unstable harvests, volatile wine and forage crops, and worsening conditions for small producers despite rising rents and land values.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Landlords and large farmers continued to prosper, but the agrarian majority experienced difficulty whose effects propagated through the whole economy.
successor_labels: Agriculture under Louis XVI—harvest instability and rural crisis

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Industry—rural production and textile dependence
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Most manufacturing, including urban-centered textiles, depended on peasant household labor and consumer demand linked to harvest outcomes.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Agriculture and industry formed an interdependent economy; cotton exports were a notable exception to erratic domestic textile markets.
successor_labels: Industry—rural production and textile dependence

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Colonial and Atlantic economy—trade, slavery, and port growth
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Sugar, coffee, and other colonial products made Caribbean possessions, especially Saint-Domingue, extraordinarily valuable and drove Atlantic commerce through slave labor and the African trade.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Colonial wealth powered major ports and overseas growth but remained weakly connected to productive development in the French interior.
successor_labels: Colonial and Atlantic economy—trade, slavery, and port growth

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: France—coastal and interior economies
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Internationally integrated coasts and lower river valleys prospered while most inland regions remained poorly connected, agrarian, and vulnerable to population pressure and climatic deterioration.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The chapter explicitly presents two French economies whose tenuous links limited the diffusion of commercial prosperity.
successor_labels: France—coastal and interior economies

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Poverty—scale, causes, and demographic pressure
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Chronic underemployment, family dependency, population growth, and wages lagging prices left roughly a third of the population poor even in good times.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Poverty is presented as a structural failure of the economy to provide secure livelihoods, not mainly a moral failure of the poor.
successor_labels: Poverty—scale, causes, and demographic pressure

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Poor relief—ecclesiastical decline and public innovation
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Traditional alms, hospitals, and poor houses lost resources while lay philanthropy, workhouses, and charitable workshops tentatively expanded.
mapping_rows.old_stance: New initiatives reflected mounting concern but remained inadequate to the growing scale of poverty.
successor_labels: Poor relief—ecclesiastical decline and public innovation

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Poverty—begging, crime, prostitution, and abandoned children
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The poor used begging, theft, smuggling, poaching, prostitution, and child abandonment as survival strategies under acute insecurity.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Contemporary elites read these behaviors as depravity, but the author locates their cause in poverty and inadequate livelihoods.
successor_labels: Poverty—begging, crime, prostitution, and abandoned children

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Peasantry—mixed livelihoods and communal rights
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Most peasant households combined small plots with wage work, cottage industry, migration, and access to commons, gleaning, and stubble grazing.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Communal resources and collective legal or direct resistance were indispensable defenses against precarity and outside encroachment.
successor_labels: Peasantry—mixed livelihoods and communal rights

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Village society—curés, coqs de village, and local power
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Parish priests and prosperous independent peasants exercised competing authority within communities stratified by land, employment, debt, and access to equipment.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Village solidarity was selective: wealthy peasants led communities and resisted outsiders but also accumulated property from poorer neighbors.
successor_labels: Village society—curés, coqs de village, and local power

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Urbanization—rural connections and uneven town growth
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Markets, cottage industry, labor migration, and demographic inflow bound towns to villages, while commercial centers grew much faster than bypassed provincial towns.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The urban-rural boundary was porous; growth concentrated wealth, literacy, and dynamism without eliminating widespread urban poverty.
successor_labels: Urbanization—rural connections and uneven town growth

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Urban labor—casual workers and domestic servants
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Unskilled urban labor was chronically oversupplied, while domestic service offered material security at the cost of dependence, celibacy, and personal autonomy.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Servants occupied a relatively privileged but tense position between the urban poor and the affluent households they served.
successor_labels: Urban labor—casual workers and domestic servants

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Guilds, apprentices, journeymen, and masters
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Skilled trades were organized through training hierarchies, journeyman mobility and compagnonnages, and guild mastership, with small workshops predominating.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Guild access was unequal but not simply closed; guilds combined quality control, worker discipline, occupational solidarity, and conflict.
successor_labels: Skilled work—guilds, journeymen and early factories

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Industrial regulation and unrest under Louis XVI
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The failed abolition of guilds, the livret, declining real wages, strikes, boycotts, and disputes with merchants made the reign increasingly contentious for artisans.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Conflict grew, but familiar guild procedures and shared craft culture could still unite masters and journeymen.
successor_labels: Industrial regulation and unrest under Louis XVI

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Bread prices, grain policy, and the Flour War
mapping_rows.old_meaning: A popular moral economy demanded affordable bread and authorized collective price-setting, while repeated deregulation of the grain trade intensified scarcity fears and riots, culminating in 1775.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Crowds were defending precarious livelihoods rather than seeking chaos; Turgot's free-market policy disastrously misread expectations and timing.
successor_labels: Bread prices, grain policy, and the Flour War

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Bourgeoisie—growth, wealth, consumption, and culture
mapping_rows.old_meaning: A rapidly expanding bourgeoisie controlled commercial and industrial capital, substantial land and public assets, and financed urban building, luxury consumption, education, print, and associations.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Bourgeois enrichment and cultural dynamism widened the visible gulf between secure elites and a growing poor population.
successor_labels: Bourgeoisie—growth, wealth, consumption, and culture

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Bourgeoisie—land purchase and withdrawal from trade
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Commercial profits were commonly transferred into land, education, professions, and status, and few families remained in trade beyond one generation.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Land promised security and prestige; praise for commerce did little to alter the entrenched drive to escape it.
successor_labels: Bourgeoisie—land purchase and withdrawal from trade

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Venal offices and the professional bourgeoisie
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The hereditary resale of public offices made government service a vast capital market and a preferred route from commerce into respectable professional life.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Officeholding provided dignity and modest security more often than great profit, while embedding purchased status throughout the state and judiciary.
successor_labels: Venal offices and the professional bourgeoisie

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Ennoblement and bourgeois social mobility
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Purchased offices, especially King's Secretaryships, enabled thousands of affluent commoners to enter the nobility and made ennoblement the summit of bourgeois success.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Mobility was substantial but strongly tilted toward wealth, provoking resentment among professional bourgeois and established nobles alike.
successor_labels: Ennoblement and bourgeois social mobility

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Bourgeois-noble tensions and barriers to public careers
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Professional commoners admired noble status but resented exclusion and moneyed leapfrogging, while pedigree requirements in parlements and the army formalized social barriers.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Measures such as the Ségur Ordinance appeared to exclude all bourgeois even when aimed at recent wealthy entrants; birth and riches displaced merit.
successor_labels: Bourgeois-noble tensions and barriers to public careers

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Nobility—status and privileges
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Nobles formed a legally separate estate marked by precedence, arms, courts, exemptions, tax advantages, and restrictions on retail trade.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Privilege was normal in a nonuniform society, but noble advantages—especially taille exemption—gave the order exceptional standing and appeal.
successor_labels: Nobility—status and privileges

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Nobility—wealth, power, and internal inequality
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Nobles collectively controlled land, seigneurial rights, offices, public debt, Church income, heavy industry, government, command, and high ecclesiastical posts, but many nobles were poor and excluded from this plutocracy.
mapping_rows.old_stance: France was governed by a wealthy elite rather than by all nobles; bourgeois fortunes continually renewed noble wealth while provincial gentry defended status without resources.
successor_labels: Nobility—wealth, power, and internal inequality

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Poor nobility and the military vocation
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Impoverished nobles claimed the army as their hereditary vocation but were priced out by purchased commissions, prompting schemes for military schools, monopoly, and merit promotion.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Reforms intended to protect committed poor nobles also preserved birth privilege and failed to displace rich courtier amateurs.
successor_labels: Poor nobility and the military vocation

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: French army—reform, organization, and social separation
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Defeat prompted Prussian-inspired reforms in tactics, uniforms, discipline, and officer formation, but the army remained internally divided and socially remote from much of France.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Professional reform did not overcome aristocratic barriers, officer indifference, regional concentration, or the exclusion of experienced men of talent.
successor_labels: French army—reform, organization, and social separation

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Army recruitment, militia, and regional military burden
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The regular army relied mainly on French volunteers from garrisoned frontiers, while unpopular militia conscription fell disproportionately on poor peasants.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Military service affected France unevenly and the army's overall weight in society was low by continental standards.
successor_labels: Army recruitment, militia, and regional military burden

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: French navy—professional competence, conscription, and expansion
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Technical demands opened naval service more widely than the army, while maritime registration supplied experienced crews and post-1763 expansion supported American independence.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Naval effectiveness improved, but the financial burden of fleets and projects such as Cherbourg contributed to state bankruptcy.
successor_labels: French navy—professional competence, conscription, and expansion

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Clergy and Church—first estate, wealth, and tax privilege
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The clergy formed the first estate, dominated worship and welfare institutions, owned extensive land and tithes, and defended exemption through representative organization and negotiated contributions.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Its institutional strength and wealth were real, but uneven distribution within the order left parish clergy carrying disproportionate burdens.
successor_labels: Clergy and Church—first estate, wealth, and tax privilege

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Church hierarchy—noble patronage and episcopal power
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Courtly patronage under the Concordat directed rich bishoprics, abbacies, and canonries toward noble families and produced politically skilled prelates.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The system privileged birth and connections over pastoral formation, though the author does not assume all bishops lacked vocation.
successor_labels: Church hierarchy—noble patronage and episcopal power

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Parish clergy—economic grievances and revolt of the curés
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Curés resented unequal Church wealth, impropriated tithes, the eroding portion congrue, clerical taxation, blocked advancement, and episcopal domination.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Royal and episcopal suppression ended assemblies but left the structural causes of lower-clergy discontent untouched.
successor_labels: Parish clergy—economic grievances and revolt of the curés

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Church reform—Jesuit expulsion and suppression of monasteries
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The 1764 expulsion of the Jesuits exposed the Church's vulnerability, and the Commission of Regulars dissolved hundreds of small contemplative houses.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Reform targeted politically weak institutions and redistributed modest assets while leaving large houses and parish-clergy problems intact.
successor_labels: Church reform—Jesuit expulsion and suppression of monasteries

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Catholic Church—religious monopoly and political power
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The established Church monopolized worship, education, much welfare, censorship, and public communication while denying most Protestants toleration and civil rights.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Its power helped sustain obedience in a lightly policed kingdom but drew unprecedented lay criticism and preserved serious religious exclusion.
successor_labels: Catholic Church—religious monopoly and political power

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Policing and public order
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Outside Paris, a very small Maréchaussée and limited urban watches enforced order, leaving everyday coercive capacity thin.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Sparse policing magnified reliance on Church authority, courts, local magistrates, and occasional troops.
successor_labels: Policing and public order

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Judicial system—venality, multiplicity, delay, and cost
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Thousands of public and private jurisdictions, staffed through venal offices and operating under nonuniform law, produced expensive disputes over competence and access to justice.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The labyrinth was widely recognized as defective but appeared insoluble without uniform law and compensation of officeholders.
successor_labels: Judicial system—venality, multiplicity, delay, and cost

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Parlements—judicial, legislative, and political opposition
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Sovereign courts combined appellate and administrative jurisdiction with registration, remonstrance, publicity, strikes, and resignations to obstruct royal policy.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Parlementary resistance delayed authority and mobilized opinion but stopped short of rebellion because the king retained the final power of lit de justice.
successor_labels: Parlements—judicial, legislative, and political opposition

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Maupeou reform and restoration of the parlements
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Maupeou exiled magistrates, abolished venality in the Paris parlement, and remodeled courts in 1771; Louis XVI reversed the reform and restored the old judiciary after his accession.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The reform failed politically despite cooperation and propaganda, while restoration repaired neither parlementary credibility nor confidence in monarchical legality.
successor_labels: Maupeou reform and restoration of the parlements

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Nobility of the robe and the administrative elite
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Sovereign-court magistrates formed a hereditary noble network that dominated provincial affairs and supplied Masters of Requests, intendants, councillors, and ministers.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Family and professional intimacy softened ordinary conflict and restricted outsiders, making Maupeou's exiles and intruders especially disruptive.
successor_labels: Nobility of the robe and the administrative elite

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Financiers, tax farming, and public credit
mapping_rows.old_meaning: A few hundred financiers collected indirect taxes, handled revenues, supplied short-term credit, and raised loans, accumulating conspicuous fortunes and influence.
mapping_rows.old_stance: They were indispensable to solvency yet widely hated because private luxury appeared to derive from public funds and fiscal oppression.
successor_labels: Financiers, tax farming, and public credit

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Versailles and the Court—patronage, dependence, and power
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Versailles concentrated courtiers around the monarch through expensive access, honors, pensions, offices, and perquisites, turning royal favor into a system of dependence and influence.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Court intrigue often looked trivial, but it distributed genuine wealth and governing power and had reconquered ministerial influence by Louis XVI's reign.
successor_labels: Versailles and the Court—patronage, dependence, and power

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Maurepas and ministerial government under Louis XVI
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Recalled from long exile, Maurepas became chief adviser and controlled appointments across the principal ministries and administrative offices until 1781.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Louis XVI relied on Maurepas's experience because he lacked other trusted guidance, even though that experience came from a less demanding political era.
successor_labels: Maurepas and ministerial government under Louis XVI

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Louis XVI—accession, character, and political inexperience
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Louis XVI inherited the throne at twenty with education, devotion, duty, and good intentions but little preparation, personal authority, or strategic direction.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The chapter closes by judging good intentions insufficient against court intrigue and acute governmental problems.
successor_labels: Louis XVI—accession, character, and political inexperience

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Arthur Young—observations on France
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Young's travel observations supply recurring contemporary judgments on regional poverty, agricultural productivity, merchant luxury, and naval construction.
mapping_rows.old_stance: His evidence is influential and often accepted with qualification; attribution access is useful because observations recur across otherwise separate subjects.
successor_labels: Arthur Young—observations on France

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Robespierre and Barnave—provincial bourgeois careers
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The early careers and remembered grievances of two future revolutionaries illustrate professional bourgeois routine, cultural aspiration, religious difference, and resentment of noble precedence.
mapping_rows.old_stance: They are examples rather than causal explanations of revolution; access should preserve their illustrative function.
successor_labels: Robespierre and Barnave—provincial bourgeois careers

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Ménétra, Jacques-Louis—journeyman mobility
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Ménétra's tour de France provides a concrete example of journeyman training, travel, guild inheritance, and compagnonnage support.
mapping_rows.old_stance: His biography is useful as a bounded illustration of artisan institutions, not a general portrait of every worker.
successor_labels: Ménétra, Jacques-Louis—journeyman mobility

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Religious conflict—Camisards and Jean Calas
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The Camisard revolt and the Calas prosecution preserved memories of sectarian violence and judicial intolerance in southern France.
mapping_rows.old_stance: These episodes are regional evidence for enduring Protestant-Catholic antagonism rather than a complete history of either event.
successor_labels: Regional Protestantism—Camisards and religious conflict

mapping_rows.rationale: Retained coherent reader requirement after owned-page review; changes and added distinctions recorded separately.
mapping_rows.old_label: Royal touch for scrofula
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Louis XVI's ritual touching of sufferers is a vivid component of coronation ritual but receives no independent development.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat as a detail under sacred kingship, not normally as a standalone access point.

mapping_rows.old_label: Peasantry—mixed livelihoods and village communities

mapping_rows.old_stance: Reject an isolated subsistence-peasant model: rural households were mobile, occupationally mixed, and connected to towns.

label.final_freeze: Restoration of the parlements and monarchical legitimacy

meaning.discovery: Louis XVI restored the old courts to signal good intentions, but suppression and restoration had exposed parlementary weakness and royal capacity for despotism, destroying the prior atmosphere of political confidence.
meaning.final_freeze: Whole-book synthesis: Louis XVI restored the old courts to signal good intentions, but suppression and restoration had exposed parlementary weakness and royal capacity for despotism, destroying the prior atmosphere of political confidence. The parlements returned amid celebration after Louis XVI's accession but squandered credit through disputes between exiled and collaborating magistrates and through limited resistance after the Turgot episode. The restored courts briefly embodied victory over despotism but lost public authority when they appeared to defend order privilege.

stance.discovery: Preserve the double damage to both courts and Crown; restoration did not return politics to its earlier state.
stance.final_freeze: Preserve the combined source qualifications: Preserve the double damage to both courts and Crown; restoration did not return politics to its earlier state. Do not treat restoration as recovery of durable constitutional authority; public confidence in the courts continued to erode. The chapter emphasizes the speed with which institutional heroes became suspect once the representation question displaced the anti-despotic consensus.

evidence.old_evidence_summary: Coronation preparations, oaths, anointing, regalia, royal touch, and court intrigue introduce the monarchy's inherited forms.
The powers, promises, and regalia are characterized as products of a long and haphazard evolution typical of the kingdom.
Population, territorial acquisitions, papal Avignon, German-princely enclaves, and Mulhouse illustrate the kingdom's historical accretion.
Provinces, 36 generalities under intendants, and 13 parlementary ressorts rarely shared boundaries.
Ecclesiastical provinces, dioceses, episcopal enclaves, and local jurisdictions multiplied the uneven pattern.
The text surveys incompatible laws, measures, tax regimes, salt-tax rates, exemptions, and internal customs barriers.
Transport, markets, advanced agriculture, population, industry, literacy, and central authority define the Paris basin as a metropolitan core.
The integrated Paris basin is contrasted with western bocage, Breton language and institutions, and outward-looking ports.
The Garonne basin and mountainous Midi present different farming systems, communications, and linguistic identities.
Alsace's German language, religious pluralism, Rhine orientation, and advanced agriculture complete the regional contrast.
Bocage, Breton identity, estates and parlement, naval and colonial ports, and the Vendée's isolation are treated together.
The Vendée's subsistence farming and low-grade textile work close the western comparison.
Rivers, maize, vineyards, petite culture, sharecropping, language, and Bordeaux's growth define the south-west.
The Massif Central's isolation, poverty, migration, and subsistence economy introduce the Midi.
Southern language, climate, crops, Protestant population, Camisards, Languedoc estates, and the Calas case receive sustained treatment.
Provence, Toulon, Marseilles, and the Rhône corridor are described as a southern commercial system.
Dauphiné migration, Lyons silk, Burgundy's vineyards and advanced works, Lorraine metallurgy, and Franche-Comté's serfdom are compared.
Alsatian Protestantism, Jewish population, German language, Rhine trade, potatoes, and intensive cultivation mark a distinct borderland.
Young's critique leads into partible inheritance, four million small owners, dispersed estates, and widespread sharecropping.
Most plots sustained families poorly and generated little surplus beyond subsistence grain.
Maize, potatoes, fertilizer scarcity, pasture, livestock, fallow, and Flanders rotations explain regional productivity differences.
Urban demand explains intensive Flanders farming and the Paris basin's large-scale leased farms.
Gros fermiers accumulated good land, enclosed fields, shifted uses, and challenged communal practices.
Transport costs, taxes, tithes, corvée, and regionally variable feudal burdens reduced agricultural returns.
The principal surviving rights and the divergence of lordship from ownership are set out.
Domaine congéable exemplifies mixed tenure whose classification became fateful in 1789.
Good harvests, population growth, and high prices gave way to frequent shortfalls and crop volatility after 1770.
Agricultural shocks reduced rural purchasing power and destabilized industrial demand.
Construction, metallurgy, and textile centers relied heavily on migrants or dispersed peasant households.
Harvest-driven demand destabilized silk, wool, and linen, while export-oriented cotton continued expanding.
Caribbean colonies, enslaved labor, the African trade, fivefold overseas growth, and booming ports form one commercial system.
The text contrasts prosperous international coastal networks with the sluggish, poorly connected interior.
Population growth and climatic deterioration eroded gains inland and raised fears about institutional resilience.
Eight million people lacked adequate employment or support, with millions more exposed in bad times as prices outran wages.
Abandonment, mortality, and insecurity are traced to the economy's inability to support the rural population.
Declining church charity and endowments are contrasted with Masonic funds, philanthropic societies, workhouses, and public workshops.
Begging, intimidation, petty theft, smuggling, poaching, and prostitution are presented as survival practices.
The growth of foundlings, overwhelmed hospitals, wet-nursing, and high child mortality reveal worsening poverty.
Peasant demographic dominance, makeshift livelihoods, seasonal migration, and communal resources are surveyed.
Communities resisted enclosure, seigneurial claims, and tithe practices through courts, riots, and passive tactics.
The curé's unifying role is contrasted with prosperous peasants who controlled jobs, credit, offices, and local resistance.
Food markets, cottage production, migration, agriculture within towns, and unequal city growth demonstrate urban-rural interdependence.
Casual trades, crowded housing, hospitals, courts, and the large servant population define the urban labor market.
Service exposed poor migrants to a more fortunate world while leaving them unable to enter it.
Apprenticeship, journeyman travel, compagnonnages, guild rules, mastership, and recruitment are explained.
Small workshops, long but self-paced work, regulation, and guild-free factories qualify the craft system.
The 1776 abolition attempt, restoration, livret, real-wage decline, worker combinations, and factory suspicion are connected.
Masters and journeymen could unite against merchants and in demands for controlled food prices.
Popular just-price beliefs, price fixing, magistrates, Paris provisioning, deregulation, famine-pact rumors, and the Flour War are narrated.
Bread's dominance in household budgets explains why respectable working people used violence to avert destitution.
The secure nonmanual elite and growing bourgeois population are placed above a precarious majority.
Capital, land, offices, architecture, luxury trades, theaters, education, books, libraries, clubs, and inequality show bourgeois weight.
Commercial fortunes at every scale moved into land, country houses, professional education, and retreat from business.
The origins of office sales and bourgeois desire to leave commerce introduce the institution.
More than 70,000 venal offices, their capital value, and the modest lives of professional families show their social function.
Thousands of ennobling offices, rapid entry into nobility, high prices, petitions, and fabricated genealogies demonstrate the pursuit of status.
Bourgeois resentment of ennobled businessmen and parlementary pedigree rules leads into the Ségur controversy.
Public formalization of noble barriers was provocative because elite education and values increasingly converged.
Debates over poor nobles and military commissions expose the conflict between birth, money, and merit.
Separate-estate status, precedence, special courts, military exemptions, and fiscal privileges are catalogued.
Trade restrictions and the intergenerational character of status reinforce nobility's governing vocation.
Noble land, offices, state investments, Church revenues, industry, and control of senior posts are surveyed.
Court wealth is contrasted with impoverished provincial gentry whose titles and seigneurial claims remained their chief assets.
Provincial gentry's poverty, trade prejudice, and contrast with robe nobles establish the problem.
Purchased commissions, public debate, military schools, and the Ségur Ordinance are framed as remedies for poor nobles.
Mid-century defeats and reforms set the institutional context.
Prussian models, service composition, limited social footprint, officer-rank distance, and blocked talent are assessed.
Foreign regiments, militia lots and exemptions, regular volunteering, desertion, army size, and regional concentration are compared.
